blocks.text: 1.5.2 Pattern Matching for instanceof (Java 14+)

The export API accepts an optional `timeout` per request. Clients report that it does nothing: a request sent with 800 ms still waits the 30-second default. The commit that rewrote the option parsing with a pattern compiled cleanly, and the default-timeout test still passes.

`o instanceof String s` tests `o`, casts it and binds the result to a new variable `s` in one step; it is standard since Java 16, after previews in 14 and 15. Unit 1.5.1 covered the test itself: the run-time class, `null`, generic types. This unit is about the variable.
A Pattern Variable Exists Only Where the Match Is Certain
Before reading the errors, guess which uses of `s` compile (the line numbers count the file's `class Scopes {` line):

Within the enclosing block, the scope follows the boolean logic: `s` exists wherever the test is known to have been true, on the right of `&&`, in the true branch of `?:`, in the `else` of a negated test. On the right of `||` the test has failed, and `&` evaluates its right side even when the left is false, so `s` doesn't exist there. After a statement, `s` exists only if the statement can't finish while the test is false. The `if (!(o instanceof String s) || s.isBlank())` falls through, so the final `return s.length()` fails. A guard clause that returns (unit 1.2.1) or a `while` loop without a `break` keeps `s` in scope for the rest of the block.

Inside its scope `s` is an ordinary local variable. It isn't implicitly final: `s = s.strip()` compiles, unless the pattern says `instanceof final String s`. Once reassigned, it is no longer effectively final, and a lambda can't capture it. A local with the same name is an error, as the last error shows. A field with the same name is not.
Out of Its Scope, a Pattern Variable's Name Means the Field
Spot the Problem: A Guard That Logs Instead of Returning
The export API's request handler, from the start of the unit:
Which `timeout` does each of the three uses read? We call it with 800 ms, then with -5 s:

800 ms:  PT30S
ignoring timeout option PT30S
-5 s:    PT30S

Only `timeout.isNegative()` reads the option. In the `if` body the test may have failed, so the pattern variable isn't in scope there. After the `if` it would be in scope only if the body couldn't complete, and this body logs and falls through. In both places the name means the field. Without the field, `cannot find symbol` (unit 1.2.1) would have caught it. With it, the class compiles under `-Xlint:all` with no warning, every request gets 30 seconds, and the log line prints the default as if it were the rejected value.
Give the guard its `return`, write the field as `this.timeout`, and log the input:

guarded 800 ms: PT0.8S
ignoring timeout option PT-5S
guarded -5 s:   PT30S
Naming the pattern variable differently from every field (`requested`) turns the original mistake back into a compile error.
<!-- practice 1 -->
A Condition Joined with && Sends a Matching Object That Fails It to the Next Branch
A payment router receives `record Payment(String account, long cents)` and `record Refund(String paymentId, long cents)` events, and was flattened from nested `if`s into one chain:

Where does a refund with no payment id go? Below, `flat` is this chain and `nested` tests each type first, with its condition inside and an `else` that returns `"dead-letter"`; the last event is a `String`:

Payment[account=acct-17, cents=4500]     flat: payments  nested: payments
Payment[account=acct-17, cents=2000000]  flat: review    nested: review
Refund[paymentId=pay-881, cents=4500]    flat: refunds   nested: refunds
Refund[paymentId=null, cents=90000]      flat: payments  nested: dead-letter
{"type":"chargeback"}                    flat: payments  nested: dead-letter

`event instanceof Refund r && r.paymentId() != null` is one boolean. When it is false, the `else` can't tell which half failed, so it receives refunds without an id as well as every other type. The comment says "the ordinary payment"; the code puts a refund that matches no payment, and a chargeback, on the `payments` queue. Give each type one branch that ends the chain for that type and put its conditions inside, or end with a test for the last type and an `else` that rejects.

A related failure is order: the first pattern that matches wins, so a supertype tested before its subtype takes every subtype object, and javac doesn't warn in an `if` chain. A `switch` over the same patterns refuses to compile (`this case label is dominated by a preceding case label`, unit 1.5.4).
<!-- practice 2 -->
Since Java 21 a Pattern of the Declared Type Compiles, and It Is Still False for null
`get` on a `Map<String, String>` returns a `String` or `null`, so `instanceof String` can only fail on `null`:

absent:  none
present: req-5c1e
null instanceof String: false

The pattern is a null check and a local variable in one, and `get` runs once. Java 16 to 20 rejected a pattern that the declared type already guarantees; Java 21 accepts it. javac 21 with `--release 17`:
Headers.java:6: error: unconditional patterns in instanceof are not supported in -source 17

"Unconditional" describes the type only. `instanceof` is false for `null` whatever the pattern, so the variable is never `null`. A reader who takes the line for a declaration and rewrites it as `String id = headers.get(...)` turns the absent header into a `NullPointerException` at `id.isBlank()`.
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **A pattern variable exists only where the match is certain.** `&&`, `?:`, the `else` of a negated test and a guard that exits extend it; `||`, `&` and a guard that falls through don't. Inside, it is an ordinary local, reassignable unless `final`.
**Out of its scope, the name means a field of the same name.** The code compiles with no warning and reads the field.
**A condition joined with `&&` sends a matching object that fails it to the next branch.** An `else` after it receives that type too, and an `if` chain never checks order.
**A pattern of the declared type compiles since Java 21 and is false for `null`.** It is a null check.

blocks.text: Challenges

items: Search your codebase for pattern variables that share a name with a field of their class. Which of them sit after a negated test whose `if` doesn't exit?
A chain tests five record types, two of them with conditions. Rewrite it so a new condition can't send objects to the wrong branch, and compare the result with a `switch` (unit 1.5.4).
Your build moves from `--release 17` to 21. Which null checks followed by a local variable would you turn into an unconditional pattern, and which would you leave as they are?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why the Scope Follows the Logic

A pattern variable could have been scoped like any declaration, to the block around it. Then `o instanceof String s && s.length() > 3` and the guard clause wouldn't work, and every use would need a nested `if`. Java scopes it by where the test is known to have been true, which lets patterns combine with `&&`, `!` and early returns, and later with `switch` and record patterns.

The cost is that one name can mean two variables in the same method, depending on the branch. When the other meaning is a field, a change to control flow, such as removing a `return`, changes which variable a line reads without any error.
